opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think of gaming and virtual worlds as really two sides of the same coin when it comes to embodied AI.

The way I frame it, there are two big pillars. One is physical embodiment, which is robotics: agents that walk, grasp, and manipulate things in the real world. The other is virtual embodiment, which is agents that live and act inside simulated worlds and games. My conviction is that eventually these converge into one model, a kind of foundation agent that can operate across many different bodies and many different realities, whether those are made of atoms or pixels.

Games matter for a few reasons. First, they're incredibly rich, open-ended environments. When we did work like MineDojo and Voyager in Minecraft, what excited me wasn't beating a benchmark. It was that Minecraft has no single objective. You can build, explore, craft, survive, and the agent has to figure out what's worth doing, keep learning, and build up a library of skills over time. That kind of open-ended, lifelong learning is exactly what we'll need for robots in the real world, and it's much cheaper and faster to prototype in a game.

Second, simulation is a data engine. In robotics, the biggest bottleneck is data. You can't scrape robot actions off the internet the way you scrape text. Real-world teleoperation is expensive and slow, limited by how many humans and robots you have and by 24 hours a day. In simulation you can run thousands of environments in parallel, far faster than real time, with randomized physics and visuals so the policy learns to generalize. We've seen with projects like Eureka that you can train surprisingly dexterous skills entirely in simulation and transfer them to the real world.

And third, longer term, I think the line between a game engine and a world model is going to blur. Today we hand-author simulators. Tomorrow, a lot of that simulation could be generated by neural networks that have learned how the world looks and behaves. Then the virtual world becomes a kind of dream space where agents can practice endlessly.

So for me, gaming isn't a side quest. It's a training ground and a proving ground. If we can build agents that are truly general in virtual worlds, we're a big step closer to agents that are general in our world.

r001.rationale: The response calls agents that live and act inside simulated worlds and games “virtual embodiment” and identifies it as one of the two pillars of embodied AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so gaming has always been close to my heart, honestly, going back to when I was a kid. But the way I think about it now is that games and virtual worlds are basically the training ground for embodied intelligence. If you look at how we got large language models to work, the secret was that the internet handed us this gigantic pre-existing dataset of human text. Robotics has no equivalent. There's no internet of physical actions lying around. You have to go out and collect the data, and collecting data on a real robot is slow, expensive, and the robot breaks.

So simulation is the way you cheat around that. In a virtual world, you can run thousands of copies of the environment in parallel, you can speed up time, you can randomize physics and lighting and textures so the agent sees a huge diversity of situations. We did some of this with Eureka and the Isaac work, where the robot learned something like pen spinning in a matter of simulation hours that would have taken forever in the real world. The game engine is essentially a data generator.

And then there's the other side, which is something like Minecraft, where I spent a lot of time with MineDojo and Voyager. Minecraft is interesting not because of physics, it's a very simple physics engine, but because it's open-ended. There's no single objective. There are millions of hours of human gameplay videos, wiki pages, Reddit threads. It's like a little internet of embodied behavior inside a game. So you can test whether an agent can explore, set its own goals, build up a library of skills, and keep going without someone telling it what to do every step. That open-endedness is exactly what you need if you want a general-purpose robot and not just a robot that does one task.

So in my mind the mission is really a continuum. Games are the sandbox where you can afford to fail a million times. Simulation is where you bring the physics closer to reality. And then at some point you transfer into a physical body. I like to think of it as the agent getting a lot of practice lives before the one that counts.

r001.rationale: The response describes games and virtual worlds as training grounds for embodied intelligence, where agents explore and act within those environments.

astra-6.text:
I see games and virtual worlds as the training ground for embodied AI. If we want an agent that can do more than talk—one that can perceive its surroundings, take actions, and learn from the consequences—we need somewhere it can practice. The physical world is slow and expensive, and mistakes can break things. In a virtual world, you can run many experiments in parallel and give an agent a huge variety of situations to learn from.

What excites me is the possibility of learning skills that generalize across worlds. Can an agent enter an unfamiliar environment, figure out how it works, and accomplish a goal? That requires perception, planning, exploration, and action working together.

Of course, doing something in a game doesn’t automatically mean you can do it with a robot. Bridging that gap is a central challenge. But I see virtual worlds as a way to build and test those capabilities at scale, with the longer-term goal of bringing them into the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response describes an agent practicing in virtual worlds by perceiving its surroundings and taking actions, framing this as training for embodied AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I see games and virtual worlds as a training ground for embodied intelligence. If we want an AI that can act—not just generate text—it needs a world where it can try things, make mistakes, and learn from the consequences. Games give us that loop, and simulation lets us run it at a scale that would be very difficult with physical robots alone.

What excites me is the diversity. You can have different bodies, different physics, different tasks, and ask whether one agent can learn skills that transfer across them. Can it explore, use tools, plan, and adapt when the environment changes?

For me, that connects directly to the mission of building general embodied agents. Virtual worlds let us develop and test those capabilities, but the real test is whether what the agent learns carries over to a new world—and eventually to a physical robot.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI agents acting, learning, and developing embodied capabilities in games and virtual worlds, identifying them as a training ground for embodied intelligence.
